summary: Analyzes actions by or against a Certification Authority or repository manager in the RPKI that could harm the internet number resources of an INR holder. It takes the perspective of the affected holder and is not meant to be comprehensive.

eli5.summary: If the keeper of the address records makes a mistake or is attacked, owners can be hurt. This lists ways that can happen.

questions: what are adverse actions in rpki
subtitle: Understanding how mistakes and attacks can harm internet number resource holders.

tldr.problem: The Resource Public Key Infrastructure helps validate routing announcements, but mistakes by Certification Authorities or repository managers, or attacks against them, can harm the internet address holders they serve.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC systematically analyzes six categories of adverse actions (deletion, suppression, corruption, modification, revocation, injection) against each RPKI object type (certificates, ROAs, manifests, CRLs), showing what an affected holder needs to watch for.
tldr.outcome: Understanding the attack surface helps RPKI operators, affected resource holders, and software developers build more robust systems and responses.

today: RFC 8211 is an Informational RFC from September 2017 that provides an operational reference for understanding RPKI security risks and remains relevant to RPKI deployment and security practices.

sections.title: Risks to Resource Holders
sections.content:
The Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) is a system that lets the owners of internet number resources (IP addresses and Autonomous System Numbers) publish and prove their ownership to make routing more secure. However, the CAs and repository managers controlling the RPKI can make mistakes, or their systems can be attacked. Any action that removes or diminishes a holder's resources without permission, or that competes with legitimate claims, is termed adverse in this RFC.

The analysis focuses on what an affected holder faces when things go wrong. This includes not just direct attacks (someone using a CA's private key) and accidents (a misconfigured certificate), but also things like legal compulsion forcing a CA to make changes. The RFC examines how these actions affect the relying parties (routers and security systems) that use RPKI data to make routing decisions.
sections.eli5: When the RPKI record keeper makes a mistake or is attacked, it can harm the real owner of an address. This RFC explains all the ways that can happen and what goes wrong.

sections.title: Six Categories of Adverse Actions
sections.content:
The RFC identifies six types of actions that can cause problems. Deletion removes an object from the repository without permission. Suppression withholds a new or updated object when the holder intends to publish it. Corruption changes a signed object in a way that breaks its signature (so it appears invalid). Modification is changing a signed object while keeping it valid, which requires the private key. Revocation places a certificate on a revocation list without permission. Injection introduces a new signed object (which requires the private key or a compromised authority).

The first three actions—deletion, suppression, and corruption—can be performed by anyone controlling the repository, including a man-in-the-middle attacker. The latter three require either access to a private key or the ability to act as a parent CA. All six can also be combined, for example revoking and deleting an object together.
sections.eli5: Bad things can happen to RPKI records in six ways: removing them, hiding them, scrambling them, changing them, revoking them, or inserting fake ones.

sections.title: Impact on RPKI Objects
sections.content:
The RFC then examines each type of RPKI object and what happens when each adverse action is performed against it. CA Certificates represent a holder in the hierarchy; changes to them can prevent subordinate objects from being found or validated. Manifests enumerate all objects at a publication point; modifying or deleting them can hide legitimate objects from relying parties. Certificate Revocation Lists (CRLs) show which certificates are no longer valid; deletion or modification can cause revoked objects to be accepted or valid ones to be rejected.

Route Origin Authorizations (ROAs) bind address space to an AS Number for origin validation; adverse actions can cause valid routes to be treated as invalid or invalid routes to be accepted. Router Certificates (used for path validation) can similarly be revoked or replaced. The analysis shows that for most object types, multiple adverse actions create distinct harmful outcomes, with some creating severe cascading effects.
sections.eli5: Each type of RPKI record can be harmed in different ways. Damaging a key record can break everything that depends on it.

sections.title: Real-World Scenarios
sections.content:
The RFC considers four scenarios showing how adverse actions can occur. Scenario A involves an unintentional mistake by a CA operator. Scenario B describes a deliberate attack where an adversary gains access to a CA's private key. Scenario C covers a compromised repository manager (without CA key access). Scenario D describes legal compulsion forcing a CA or manager to make adverse changes.

These scenarios help clarify which types of protection matter: CAs need good operational security and key management; repository managers need access controls; and relying parties need to monitor for suspicious changes and maintain alternative data sources or cached copies. Understanding the scenarios helps operators prioritize which protections are most important for their deployment.
sections.eli5: The RFC thinks about four ways things could go wrong: oops, hack, inside threat, or legal pressure. Each one needs different defenses.
